title: Indus Valley Civilization
shortDescription: A planned urban world of craft, trade and remarkable civic order.
description: Around five thousand years ago, communities along the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra systems built some of the earliest cities in South Asia. Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira reveal carefully planned streets, standardized bricks, craft workshops and long-distance trade.

title: Great Bath of Mohenjo-Daro
shortDescription: A precisely engineered brick tank at the heart of an ancient city.
description: The Great Bath is a sunken pool built with finely fitted baked bricks and sealed with bitumen. Steps descend from both ends, while surrounding rooms suggest that bathing was more than a practical act: it may have held social or ritual significance. This interactive model shows the bath together with its surrounding archaeological setting.
keyFacts: Built in the Mature Harappan period
Located inside a large citadel complex
Water was likely drawn from nearby wells

title: Ashoka Pillar
shortDescription: Polished stone, ethical edicts and the lion capital that became a national symbol.
description: Emperor Ashoka placed inscribed pillars across his empire in the third century BCE. Their messages, written in Prakrit and often using Brahmi script, urged compassion, restraint and respect among communities. The Sarnath capital’s four lions now appear on India’s state emblem.
keyFacts: Many pillars were carved from Chunar sandstone
The Sarnath lions inspired the State Emblem

title: Nalanda University
shortDescription: A cosmopolitan centre of Buddhist philosophy, logic, medicine and mathematics.
description: Nalanda grew into one of the ancient world’s great residential centres of learning in present-day Bihar. Monasteries, lecture spaces and libraries drew students and teachers from across Asia, creating a culture of debate and translation that lasted for centuries.
keyFacts: Active from at least the fifth century CE
Located near modern Rajgir and Bihar Sharif
Welcomed scholars from China and Korea
The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site
